Rule. Hold this rule for Facade: Offer one operation in front of a sequence the caller should not orchestrate. Say it before you pick a tool from Design patterns.

Why it matters. Interviewers on the Design patterns track listen for whether you can name the idea facade and refuse the common wrong pick. The summary is the force: Offer one operation in front of a sequence the caller should not orchestrate. If you cannot restate it, you will drift into product names or trivia.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a prompt lands that fits Facade. You restate the force in one sentence — Offer one operation in front of a sequence the caller should not orchestrate. — then show a tiny walkthrough that would fail if you ignored that force. You label the SAMPLE answer with the cost or the tradeoff, not with a brand name.

When to use. Use Facade when the prompt's access pattern or force matches the summary above, when a prior slug in its after-list is already in hand, and when saying the rule changes which next step you take.

When to refuse. Refuse Facade when a simpler tool already covers the force, when a prerequisite in after is still missing, or when applying it would invent a mechanism the track never taught. Prefer naming the missing slug over bluffing.
